Ten micrometres · live plasma flow with elastic cells

Inside a Drop of Blood

A drop of blood holds about five million red cells per microlitre, each a soft bag of haemoglobin wider than the narrowest vessels it must pass. Here the plasma is a real fluid simulation and every cell is an elastic membrane with the measured stiffness of a red cell, solved together on your graphics card.

Field guide

What's in a drop

A microlitre of blood, a cube one millimetre on a side, holds about five million red cells, five to ten thousand white cells and a few hundred thousand platelets, all carried by plasma. These are the players in the simulation above and the numbers it is built on.

7.8 µm across · 4.2–6.2 million per µL

The red cell: a bag with spare skin

A red cell holds 94 µm³ of haemoglobin solution inside 135 µm² of membrane. A sphere of that volume would need only 100 µm², so the cell has a third more skin than it needs. That slack is why it can fold into almost any shape without stretching: its membrane resists change of area strongly but shearing hardly at all.

5–7 µm wide · 0.5–1 mm long

The capillary

Capillaries are narrower than the cells they carry. Cells pass in single file, folded into parachutes (Skalak & Brånemark filmed them in 1969: a biconcave disc with its upstream face pushed in), at 0.2–1.5 mm/s. A red cell can get through a tube as narrow as about 2.7 µm.

plasma 1.1–1.3 mPa·s · inside a cell about 5.6

The cell-free layer

In any vessel wider than a capillary, the cells drift away from the wall, leaving a sleeve of plain plasma 1–2 µm thick. The cell-rich core slides on it. This is why blood in small vessels is thinner, and carries fewer cells, than blood in big ones.

shear modulus 5–10 µN/m

How soft is a red cell?

Pulled between two glass beads with laser tweezers, a cell stretches from 7.8 to about 16 µm under 0.2 nanonewtons (Mills et al. 2004). Stiffness is health: one study found stored blood stiffening about fivefold in three weeks in the bag. Make the cells stiffer here and the soft parachute becomes a bullet that needs more pressure to push.

irreversibly sickled cells: 20 µN/m vs 7 healthy

Sickle cell disease

Haemoglobin S polymerises when it loses oxygen, but only after a delay that shortens roughly as the 30th power of its concentration (Hofrichter, Ross & Eaton 1974). Delays span the capillary transit time, so many cells escape before they stiffen; those that don't, and the cells left permanently sickled, are what block vessels.

P. falciparum: up to 10× stiffer

Malaria and the spleen

As the parasite grows, its host cell stiffens: about 18 µN/m at the ring stage, 36 at the trophozoite, against 7 for a healthy cell (Mills et al. 2007), and the ring stage stiffens further to 30 at a fever of 41 °C. The spleen strains blood through narrow slits, and holds back the cells that won't bend.

4,500–11,000 white cells · 150,000–400,000 platelets per µL

The rest of the traffic

A neutrophil is a sphere of about 300 µm³, some 8 µm across, that crawls at around 18 µm a minute; in David Rogers' 1950s film one chases a staphylococcus, a bacterium 1 µm across, through a blood smear. Platelets are discs 2–3 µm wide. Both get pushed to the wall by the red cells, which is where they are needed. They are not simulated here.

The Fåhræus–Lindqvist effect

Why blood gets thinner in narrow vessels

In 1931 Robin Fåhræus and Torsten Lindqvist pushed blood through glass tubes and found that below about 0.3 mm it flows more easily the narrower the tube; later work traced the trend down to about 7 µm. The reason is the cell-free layer: the narrower the tube, the larger the fraction of it taken up by the slippery plasma sleeve. The same sleeve lets the cells move faster than the plasma on average, so a narrow tube holds fewer cells than the blood flowing through it (the Fåhræus effect).

Narrow tubes are easier to push blood through, until the cells no longer fit.

Each simulated dot has its own share of cells leaving the tube, between 21% and 26%, so it belongs next to the blue curve. On the fine grid the simulated thickness is within 0–9% of the experiments. The live arteriole above runs on a grid twice as coarse so that it moves at a watchable pace, and reads 15–20% thick: the force-spreading kernel makes each cell act a little bigger than it is. To see the fine grid itself, record a fine-grid replay: the page computes a short stretch of the 20 µm arteriole on the 0.25 µm grid, as fast as your graphics card can, then plays it back with the camera free. It reads about 1.32× against the glass-tube 1.25×.

What the simulation gets less well is the Fåhræus effect: in glass tubes the cells crowd towards the fast centre more than they do here, so the ratio of cells in the tube to cells leaving it is 0.71 here and 0.62 in experiments.

Honest numbers

Checked against experiments

Before any graphics, each part of the model was run headless and compared with measurements or exact theory: first the membrane alone, then the fluid alone, then the two together, then crowds of cells.

Most of it agrees within a few per cent. The places where it doesn't are listed too: a red cell pulled by laser tweezers narrows less than real ones do at low force, the cells crowd toward the middle of a tube less than in glass-tube experiments, and the live arteriole's coarse grid reads 15–20% thick.

Sources: Evans & Fung 1972; Mills et al. 2004 (via Suresh 2005 data); Barthès-Biesel & Rallison 1981 and Krüger et al. 2011; Pries et al. 1992; Fedosov et al. 2010 (Microcirculation 17:615).

How it works

A fluid, some elastic bags, and a handshake

lattice Boltzmann · 0.25–0.5 µm cells

The plasma

Space is divided into a grid of cubes a quarter or half a micrometre on a side, up to a few million of them. In each, 19 numbers track how much fluid is moving in each of 19 directions; every time step they stream to the neighbouring cube and relax toward equilibrium. That simple rule reproduces the Navier–Stokes equations of a viscous fluid. Walls bounce the fluid back at their exact curved position.

642 or 2,562 points per cell

The cells

Each cell is a closed mesh of triangles with the measured elasticity of red-cell membrane: a shear modulus of 5.3 µN/m, a strong resistance to changing area, a bending stiffness of 2×10⁻¹⁹ J, and a fixed volume. The resting biconcave shape is the one it relaxes back to. Inside, the cytoplasm is five times more viscous than plasma.

the immersed-boundary method

The handshake

The membrane and the fluid never share a grid. Each step, every membrane point spreads its elastic force onto the nearby fluid cubes; the fluid moves; then every point moves at the fluid's local speed. Membrane and plasma move together, so the cell carries its contents and the plasma flows around it.

why time is slowed

Keeping it watchable

At this size, flow is so slow and viscous that only ratios matter: how hard the flow pulls compared with how stiff the cell is. The simulation keeps those ratios but lets the plasma carry about a thousand times more inertia than real blood, which lets each step cover more time. The flow is still dominated by viscosity, and quartering the inertia changed the results by under 1%.

every step, on your graphics card

Seven passes per step

Measure each cell's area and volume; compute the force on every membrane point; find nearby points of other cells (so cells never pass through each other); spread the forces into the fluid; advance the fluid; and move the membranes. A fast graphics card does this thousands of times a second.

what is left out

Limits

No membrane viscosity, no sticking to the vessel wall, no clumping into rouleaux, no living machinery: a white cell's crawling and a parasite's knobs are beyond it. The sickled cells keep the stiffness measured for oxygenated ones; fully deoxygenated cells are far stiffer than this model can step stably.

Inside a Drop of Blood is part of a series of live simulations walking down the scales of nature: The Cosmic Web, Bridges & Tails, Event Horizon, The Chirp, The Clockwork, The Atmosphere, The Wind Tunnel, and now ten micrometres, between the flow around a cyclist and the molecules of The Hydrogen Bond and The Quantum Atom.
